html:
Every Salesforce project is a change to how people work, and the people it changes are stakeholders. This phase teaches you to find them, classify them, engage them proportionally, and run the Discovery interviews and workshops that produce honest requirements. The running case is the BrightLogistics CRM rollout, where a founder, sales reps, dispatchers, and a skeptical finance owner all have a stake.

Learning Objectives

  • Identify and classify stakeholders by power and interest and plan proportional engagement...
  • Create a RACI matrix for a Salesforce initiative with one Accountable per activity...
  • Plan and run structured discovery interviews with active listening and agreed notes...
  • Facilitate a discovery workshop with one facilitator and one scribe...
  • Manage stakeholder expectations, conflicts, and scope creep early...
  • Use the Stakeholder__c object and RSVP Tracking Flow in the lab...

1. Why Stakeholder Management Precedes Everything

The CBA exam weights Collaboration and Communication at 23% — the largest knowledge area — and it is not an accident. A perfectly designed Org is worthless if the people who must adopt it were never consulted, informed, or given a reason to care. Stakeholder management is not a soft skill bolted onto the analysis; it is the analysis: the requirements you write in Phase 4 are commitments extracted from stakeholders here.

Stakeholders withhold disagreement — the dispatcher who says "looks fine to you" and then routes the old way in production. Discovery done well makes objections loud early, where they cost nothing. The senior dispatcher opposes auto-assignment because she fears the system "will pick the wrong carrier": found in Discovery, a training and trust requirement; found after go-live, a failed KPI.

2. Identifying Stakeholders: The Source Map

Before you can map stakeholders, you must find them all. Start with the org chart, then go beyond: sales reps, dispatchers, billing, the compliance person who signs carrier agreements, the IT admin who will run the org, and the client-facing staff who deliver bad news when a load is late. Anyone who influences the project, is affected by it, or holds information it needs is a stakeholder.

The fastest way to complete the list is to let it build itself. End every interview and workshop with "who else should I talk to?" — the best source map comes from stakeholders themselves. Greg names the dispatcher team; the dispatchers name the billing clerk keeping the lead log in a spreadsheet no one else knows exists. Each new name triggers a quick classification: decision-maker, contributor, approver, or informant. For a 40-person company, expect a source map of twelve to eighteen people — exactly the scale Discovery should cover.

3. Power vs Interest Mapping

Power and interest are the two axes that decide engagement. Power is the ability to influence the project's outcome — funding it, stopping it, overriding decisions. Interest is how much the stakeholder cares about the project and its results. Classify everyone high or low on both axes, then place them on the grid.

QuadrantEngagementExample on BrightLogistics
High power, high interestManage closelyGreg Nweshi, executive sponsor
High power, low interestKeep satisfiedFinance owner funding the rollout
Low power, high interestKeep informedDispatcher end-users, client-facing staff
Low power, low interestMonitorCasual observer, adjacent departments

The grid is deliberately coarse — four buckets, not a scatterplot. Its purpose is to stop you spending effort in the wrong place. Keep-satisfied stakeholders get milestone updates and decision-point involvement, not weekly minutiae. Keep-informed stakeholders get summaries and early demos, because their enthusiasm is your change-management engine. Monitor stakeholders get an occasional glance, a quarterly note that the project exists.

4. Reading the Quadrants and Choosing Engagement

Each quadrant has a distinct trap. Managing the high-power, high-interest sponsor too loosely starves the project of decisions; too tightly turns every requirement into a chess move. Greg is the client for trust and the arbiter of scope — he approves the sub-4-hour dispatch KPI and can pull funding. He gets a one-page status aligned to business outcomes at every milestone, nothing thicker.

The finance owner sits high-power, low-interest: able to stop the project at a capital review but unlikely to care how many fields the Lead record has. That proximity to power with low interest is risky; the engagement is "keep satisfied" — involve them at decision points about money or timeline, never in the sprint logs. The dispatchers, by contrast, are low-power, high-interest end-users: demos, training previews, and a visible feedback channel. They are the future champions or the future saboteurs, and the choice is made during Discovery.

5. The Stakeholder Engagement Plan

The one-page engagement plan turns the grid into action: per stakeholder, record quadrant, strategy, cadence, and method. A typical row reads "Finance owner — keep satisfied — monthly during capital review — one-page PDF." Matching the cadence to the delivery cadence — weekly for manage-closely, monthly for keep-satisfied, per-release for keep-informed — keeps the plan real.

The lab models this. The Stakeholder__c custom object (force-app/main/default/objects/Stakeholder__c/) carries the dimensions the drama needs: Influence__c and Interest__c picklists, Power_Score__c and Interest_Score__c numerics, Engagement_Level__c for the strategy, and RACI__c for the role. StakeholderEngagementService in force-app/main/default/classes/StakeholderEngagementService.cls steers the engagement level from the scores — the classifier you should be able to run by hand on the exam.

6. RACI in Practice

Where the power/interest grid says how to engage, RACI says who does what. Every activity gets one Responsible (the doer), one Accountable (the answerable one), and any number of Consults and Informs.

md
| Activity            | Sponsor | PM | Business Owner | SME | IT |
|---------------------|---------|----|----------------|-----|----|
| Prioritize backlog  | A       | I  | R              | C   | C  |
| Define requirements | C       | A  | R              | R   | C  |
| Design data model   | I       | A  | C              | R   | R  |
| Execute UAT         | I       | R  | A              | C   | I  |

Read the people, not just the letters. The Sponsor is Accountable for backlog priorities but only Informs on UAT — the Business Owner owns the UAT outcome while the PM runs it. Such a matrix answers the two questions that stall projects: "who decides?" is always the single A, "who does the work?" always the single R.

7. One Responsible, One Accountable: RACI Guardrails

Two As for one activity is the number-one RACI smell: when a review stalls on a hard call, two accountable owners each wait for the other. Resolve to one Accountable before the matrix goes out. The same applies to the R — two Responsible people means the task is underspecified, so split the activity until each has one doer.

A second guardrail is honesty about Accountable vs Responsible. The classic inverted matrix puts the PM as Accountable for everything, making the PM a single point of failure and quietly removing business ownership. On BrightLogistics UAT, the Business Owner is Accountable and the PM Responsible — deliberately. The same gate appears in Phase 4, where the Business_Requirement__c approval process names one approver per requirement: the data model enforces the same one-A rule the matrix does.

8. Planning a Structured Interview

A discovery interview is a one-on-one, usually 30 to 60 minutes, driven by a prepared guide. The guide opens broad and narrows: warm-up, current work, pain points, success criteria, closing prompt. Build it around open questions ("walk me through what happens after a lead arrives"), one topic at a time — never bundle two questions into one sentence, because the second answer gets lost.

Preparation is the difference between a chat and discovery. Read the artifacts the stakeholder already produces — lead log, dispatch spreadsheet, complaint emails — before you sit down. Three questions do most of the work: "what happens today?", "what breaks?", and "what would success look like?" A fourth, "who else should I talk to?", completes the source map. For Greg, push the conversation past the 48-hour dispatch problem to the strategic why — why now, why Salesforce, what changes if this fails.

9. Running the Interview: Listen 80%, Talk 20%

The ratio is the discipline: listen 80%, talk 20%. Talking means asking, clarifying, and mirroring back — never lecturing about your favorite features. Mirroring is the active-listening technique that keeps interviews honest: restate what you heard in your own words and let the stakeholder correct you. "You're saying leads sit in a shared inbox until the morning shift reads it — did I get that right?" That habit catches half of all misunderstandings before they become requirements.

Take notes on facts, not opinions. Quotes verbatim are evidence ("I re-type every lead"); judgments ("the team is slow") are not. Log what you do not know as open questions instead of guessing. And resist solving: a stakeholder describing a broken process is offering a map, not inviting a proposed solution. Collect everything, synthesize after.

10. After the Interview: Notes, Thanks, and the 24-Hour Rule

The interview is unfinished until it is written up. Within 24 hours, send the stakeholder a thank-you with a summary of the discussion, the decisions recorded, and the open questions. The rule matters three ways: it confirms understanding while the conversation is fresh, it gives the stakeholder a written artifact to correct, and it keeps the project visible — every interview is also a small communication campaign.

Your notes become discovery inputs: facts for the Phase 3 process maps, source links for Phase 4 requirements, and origins for the traceability matrix. When a requirement is challenged, the BA answers "where did that come from?" with an interview name and a date, not a shrug — the dispatcher's re-keying complaint should trace to a dated note that feeds both "eliminate manual re-entry of web leads" and the 80% auto-assignment KPI.

11. Facilitating Discovery Workshops

A workshop batches discovery: 45 to 90 minutes, at most 12 people, one facilitator and one scribe. The facilitator drives the agenda and energy; the scribe captures what is decided on the wall — whiteboard, sticky notes, or Miro. Two people because the facilitator running the room cannot also write fast enough to be trustworthy.

Ground rules make the workshop safe and fast: phones away, tangents go to a visible parking lot, and decisions get made on the spot. Use structured voting — sticky dots — to find consensus on pain points. A BrightLogistics lead-intake workshop with two dispatchers, a sales rep, and ops should produce the as-is lead journey (raw material for the Phase 3 swimlane), the ranked list of what breaks, and a parking lot of feature ideas. The RSVP flow in force-app/main/default/flows/Stakeholder_RSVP_Tracking.flow-meta.xml and StakeholderRSVPService record who confirmed — attendance data is governance data when you must show the right people were consulted.

12. Managing Expectations and Conflict Early

Expectations default to a wish list. Managing them means converting hopes into written scope: what the project will and will not deliver, and when. The cleanest tool is a crisp problem statement plus a KPI — BrightLogistics is not "build us a portal," it is "get leads to a dispatcher in under 4 hours." Anything that does not serve the KPI goes to the backlog or the out-of-scope list, and saying no with a reason is a service, not a rejection.

Conflict, too, is earlier-better. When sales wants routing by rep and operations by region, the tension stays in Discovery until a decision rule appears. The BA's job is not to take sides but to surface the decision, attach it to a stakeholder (usually the RACI's Accountable), and record the outcome — the Stakeholder__c RACI field and the requirement's source link preserve it so the fight is not replayed every sprint.

13. The Lab: Stakeholder__c, RSVP Tracking, and Engagement Scoring

Put it into practice. Deploy the metadata, open Stakeholder__c, and create a record for each BrightLogistics stakeholder with Influence__c, Interest__c, and RACI__c set. Watch StakeholderEngagementService derive Engagement_Level__c from the two scores — the grid in code — and run the Stakeholder_RSVP_Tracking Flow so invitee RSVP_Status__c moves from Invited to Confirmed.

apex
// StakeholderEngagementService: quadrants become data
Stakeholder__c fin = new Stakeholder__c(
  Name = 'Finance Owner', Influence__c = 'High',
  Interest__c = 'Low',  RACI__c = 'Accountable' // funding gates
);
// Service derives Engagement_Level__c = 'Keep Satisfied'

Expected outcomes: a dozen-plus stakeholder records with distinct engagement levels, an RSVP dashboard showing attendance, and a filterable RACI segment — raw material for Phase 3's maps and Phase 4's traceable requirements. A stakeholder never logged is a requirement that cannot be sourced.

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 2.1: Power/Interest Grid for BrightLogistics

  1. List the BrightLogistics stakeholders: Greg Nweshi, the sales and operations team, the dispatcher who reads the inbox, the finance owner, and the IT admin who will run the org.
  2. Assign each a High or Low Influence__c and Interest__c value, then place them in one of the four quadrants.
  3. Write the one-sentence engagement strategy per quadrant, and name which stakeholder could silently block the project from each quadrant.

Expected result: a four-quadrant grid with a tactic per quadrant and a named highest-risk stakeholder (likely the finance owner or the senior dispatcher). What it proves: you can classify stakeholders and allocate attention proportionally. Pairs with Exercise 2.1 Power-interest grid in Phase 15.

Exercise 2.2: RACI Matrix for the Lead-Intake Release

  1. Take six BrightLogistics release activities: define KPI, document as-is process, design data model, build routing, execute UAT, train dispatchers.
  2. Assign each activity exactly one R and one A plus any C/I, using the roles Sponsor, PM, Business Owner, SME, IT.
  3. Check yourself: two As on one activity means rework; a PM as A for everything means the business is not owning outcomes.
  4. Record the roles in the RACI__c field of the matching Stakeholder__c records.

Expected result: a 6-row RACI matrix that passes the one-A, one-R rule, plus stakeholder records carrying their RACI roles. What it proves: you can translate a matrix into the data model the lab uses for role governance. Pairs with Exercise 2.2 RACI matrix in Phase 15.

Exercise 2.3: Interview Guide and Mock Discovery for Greg

  1. Write a 45-minute interview guide for Greg with open questions only, one topic per question, ending with "what would success look like?" and "who else should I talk to?".
  2. Role-play 10 minutes with a partner: they talk, you listen 80/20 and mirror twice.
  3. Within 24 hours, produce a one-page summary: facts, quotes, decisions, open questions.

Expected result: a guide, a mirrored listening transcript, and a dated one-page summary that would survive being sent to Greg for correction. What it proves: you can run the full interview loop — prepare, listen, mirror, and write up. This pairs with Exercise 2.3 Discovery interview in Phase 15.

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
StakeholderAnyone who influences the project, is affected by it, or holds information the project needs.
PowerAbility to influence the project's outcome — fund it, stop it, or override decisions.
InterestHow much the stakeholder cares about the project and its results.
Source mapThe stakeholder list revealed by asking every contact "who else should I talk to?".
Manage closelyEngagement for high-power, high-interest stakeholders: frequent, decision-aligned.
Keep satisfiedEngagement for high-power, low-interest stakeholders: milestones and decisions only.
Keep informedEngagement for low-power, high-interest stakeholders: summaries, demos, feedback channels.
RACIA matrix of one Responsible, one Accountable, plus Consults and Informs per activity.
Interview guidePrepared open, single-topic questions that drive a discovery interview.
Active listeningListening 80%, talking 20%, mirroring back what the stakeholder said.
24-hour ruleThank-you and summary notes within 24 hours of any interview or workshop.
Parking lotA visible list where tangents are parked so the agenda stays on track.

Certification Checkpoints

  • I can place any stakeholder on a power/interest grid and name the engagement strategy.
  • I can build a RACI matrix with exactly one Accountable and one Responsible per activity and list the BrightLogistics highest-risk quadrant.
  • I can write an interview guide with open, single-topic questions and run an 80/20 interview, mirroring and writing up notes within 24 hours.
  • I can plan a 45-90 minute workshop with roles, ground rules, and voting.
  • I can create Stakeholder__c records with power/interest scores and RACI roles in the lab.
  • I can explain why Collaboration and Communication is 23% of the CBA blueprint.

Summary

You learned to find stakeholders through source mapping, classify them on the power/interest grid, and choose proportional engagement for each quadrant. You built RACI matrices that follow the one-A, one-R rule and practiced the discovery loop: interview guide, 80/20 listening, mirroring, and agreed notes within 24 hours. The lab models all of it — the Stakeholder__c object, the engagement-scoring service, and the RSVP Flow — so the people side of analysis leaves a data trail that feeds every later phase.
